hints: Look closely at the diagram and notice that every second beta-glucose is flipped upside down, so the OH on carbon 2 points up in one unit and down in the next.
Remember that OH groups can form hydrogen bonds, not new glycosidic bonds, and think about what pointing both up and down lets one chain do with the chains lying above and below it.
walkthrough:
**Spot the flip in the diagram**

Look at the OH on carbon 2 in the four rings. In the 1st and 3rd it points up, in the 2nd and 4th it points down.

This happens because each beta-glucose is rotated 180 degrees to allow the 1-4 glycosidic bond to form. The chain stays beautifully straight.

**Recall the two types of bond**

Glycosidic bonds join glucose monomers together within one cellulose chain. They are strong covalent bonds formed by condensation.

Hydrogen bonds are weak bonds that form between OH groups. In cellulose they form between separate parallel chains, not within the glycosidic backbone.

**Link opposite sides to strength**

Because OH groups stick out on both sides of the chain, one cellulose chain can form hydrogen bonds upwards to one neighbour and downwards to another neighbour.

Many chains therefore become cross-linked into bundles called microfibrils, giving cellulose its huge tensile strength for cell walls. That matches option D.

options.A: Cross-links between cellulose chains are only hydrogen bonds. Glycosidic bonds only join monomers within a single chain.
options.B: Glycosidic bonds never form between separate cellulose molecules, only between glucose units in the same chain.
options.C: The key strength comes from bonds between different cellulose chains, not just between adjacent glucose units in the same chain.
options.D: Alternating OH positions allow hydrogen bonding on both sides of the chain to OH and CH2OH groups of neighbouring chains, holding microfibrils together.
